Dubrovnik Old Jewish Cemetery

Jewish Cemetery · Dubrovnik, Croatia

Demolished. Dubrovnik (historically Ragusa), a major Adriatic trading city since the 7th century, took its current Slavic name in the 11th century; its Jewish history began in the 14th century with Italian merchants and doctors, though residence was officially forbidden. A formal ghetto (11 houses, interconnected without needing to step outside) was established in 1546, home by the 16th century to a flourishing community of about 250, mostly refugees from the Spanish and Portuguese expulsions, active in trade, banking, and scholarship - notably Rabbi Aaron ben David (1610-1656). The 17th century brought Church-driven persecution, including a 1724 public Talmud burning ordered by the city Senate; equal rights only came under Austrian rule at the century's end, with ghetto status formally abolished in 1808. Population fell to 121 by 1857 and just 120 (of 30,000 residents) by the 1930s. Italian occupation during WWII briefly shielded the community (87 local Jews plus 1,600 Croatian refugees) until Italy's 1943 capitulation, after which Croatian nationalists deported most to concentration camps - only 23 survived. This original cemetery, built in 1652 near the northern ramparts, was sold at the end of the 19th century, with its graves transferred to the newer Boninovo cemetery in 1911; a 2011 archaeological excavation uncovered additional old tombstones repurposed to line a drainage canal.
